fieldData.name: Municipal Waste Finance in Africa: Collection Contracts, Recycling Revenues and Public Service
fieldData.standfirst: A city can contain valuable discarded materials and still lack the money to collect its rubbish. Africa's circular-economy opportunity depends on recognising that difference. Recent collection reforms in Kampala, project preparation in Senegal and South African packaging-finance arrangements show why reliable services need an explicit payer, an accountable operating chain and a fair settlement with the people already recovering materials.
fieldData.subtitle: Comparing Kampala, Senegal and South African packaging finance to assess the conditions for reliable urban waste services
fieldData.hero-caption: StoneComms conceptual illustration of municipal waste collection and material recovery in an African city; not a named facility.
fieldData.hero-alt-text: African waste workers move a covered bin and check sorted cardboard beside a collection truck and neighbourhood recovery bay.
fieldData.article-body:
EXECUTIVE THESIS

  • Fund collection and controlled disposal as continuing services; assess material recovery as a separate commercial activity.
  • Distinguish announced vehicle capacity, procured infrastructure and verified operating performance.
  • Include existing waste workers in contract design before changing access to materials or collection routes.

StoneComms original synthesis: Municipal waste finance should maintain two connected accounts: a service account showing who pays for collection, transport and safe residual management, and a materials account showing the net proceeds from specific recoverable products. Combining them without disclosing transfers can conceal an unfunded service obligation behind a promising recycling market.

The question is not whether recycling has value. It is whether that value is available to the entity responsible for the service, after sorting losses, transport, processing and payment delays. This distinction matters to municipalities awarding contracts, financiers assessing facilities and producers financing packaging recovery.

WHY THIS MATTERS NOW

The World Bank's 2026 What a Waste 3.0 brings together information on 217 countries and economies and 262 cities. Its accompanying catalogue warns that definitions and reporting quality vary, with individual observations drawn from different sources. The new reference base improves the questions cities can ask; it is not a harmonised November 2026 census of African waste services. [1, 2]

Two recent developments make the financing question concrete. Kampala Capital City Authority announced an expanded private collection network on 14 August 2026. In Senegal, PROMOGED reported on 6 October that it had shared feasibility and preliminary PPP-assessment findings for Dakar-region waste infrastructure. These are different stages of institutional work, rather than comparable demonstrations of completed performance. [3, 4]

The investment decision should follow that distinction. Buying trucks, commissioning a recovery facility and sustaining a citywide collection service are related commitments, but they have different operating risks and payment requirements. A capital budget cannot substitute for the recurring revenue needed after equipment arrives.

WHAT THE THREE CASES ESTABLISH

Kampala: authorised capacity and actual collection are different measures

KCCA's August announcement described nine private collectors, of which eight had operational licences and the ninth awaited final zone allocation. The authority reported combined evacuation capacity exceeding 2,100 tonnes a day when its own fleet was included. This was an estimate of capacity, not independently verified daily tonnage collected and safely managed. [3]

KCCA also set out differentiated household charges and retained responsibility for government common-user facilities, including public markets and health centres. Its 2025 client charter describes a weekly household service and corresponding bag-based charges. These documents establish a service and payment design; they do not demonstrate payment compliance, affordability or consistent route coverage. [3, 5]

The useful preparation question is therefore operational: what proportion of scheduled collections actually occurs, who is missed, where does the load go and when is the operator paid? A bag charge may be administratively simple but still needs arrangements for households unable to pay and for places ordinary vehicles cannot reach.

KCCA's August announcement also prohibited certain small collection vehicles, including handcarts and wheelbarrows. The authority presents this as part of formalising the system. StoneComms has not established its effect on workers or access in narrow streets; those consequences require examination rather than an assumption that larger licensed capacity automatically improves every neighbourhood's service. [3]

Senegal: appraise the whole operating chain

PROMOGED's published programme describes pre-collection, collection, recycling, transfer, treatment and disposal, alongside institutional and financing reform. Its planned work includes progressive improvement of Mbeubeuss and facilities across several urban poles. This is a programme design, not evidence that every listed facility is complete. [6]

The October 2026 workshop addressed feasibility and prior appraisal of a possible PPP for Dakar-region waste infrastructure. Sharing studies is a preparation milestone, not an award, financial close or operational start. The sources reviewed do not disclose the contract terms needed to assess the proposed allocation of commercial and fiscal risk. [4]

PROMOGED separately describes livelihood-restoration and resettlement plans associated with Mbeubeuss. This makes the transition of existing recoverers part of the project boundary. A published plan demonstrates that an issue is recognised; it does not establish that compensation is adequate, livelihoods are restored or participation is effective. [7]

For other cities, the transferable idea is an integrated appraisal boundary. A transfer station may reduce long-haul vehicle time, yet add handling costs and dependence on another operator. A recovery plant may need cleaner feedstock than mixed collection delivers. Each interface needs an operating agreement and a funded fallback, not merely a position in a master plan.

South African packaging: a distinct source of recovery finance

Petco's published 2026 schedule differentiates fees by packaging category. Its explanation of net cost recovery includes collection, transport, storage, treatment, administration, communication and oversight, with material-sale revenues deducted. This is a producer-responsibility organisation's account of its own scheme; it is not a national audit of municipal waste finance. [8]

The important financial distinction is that a producer fee can remunerate recovery services in addition to commodity sales. It should not be treated as a universal entitlement for all waste or every municipal operator. Eligibility, product scope, contracts, evidence and payment conditions must be established for the specific scheme.

A city considering a similar arrangement needs to identify which products are covered, which actor receives payment, and which costs remain with the public service. Packaging recovery can have a credible financing mechanism while organics, contaminated materials and final residuals still require separate funding. A functioning material market cannot be assumed to finance the entire waste stream.

KampalaLicensed collection expansion, estimated evacuation capacity and differentiated charges.Actual sustained coverage, payment performance and safe management of every collected load.
SenegalIntegrated programme design and PPP-preparation activity; worker-transition plans.Completed facilities, final contract allocation and realised livelihood outcomes.
South African packagingA published producer-fee mechanism covering defined recovery costs.Universal municipal coverage or a surplus available to finance all waste services.

TWO ACCOUNTS FOR ONE SYSTEM

  • The service account records obligations, operating costs and dependable payments.
  • The materials account records recoverable outputs, buyers and net realisations.
  • Transfers between the accounts must be explicit and stress-tested.

StoneComms original synthesis: UNEP's Global Waste Management Outlook 2024 identifies a persistent gap between material value and full system cost, and stresses continuing operating expenditure. Combining that evidence with Kampala's service charges, Senegal's integrated infrastructure plans and Petco's recovery-finance mechanism yields a practical distinction: finance the public obligation, then test which recovery revenues can reliably contribute. Confidence is moderate as a preparation framework; comparable audited project cash flows were not available. [3, 6, 8, 9]

The service account

Specify the population and premises covered, collection frequency, access arrangements, transfer capacity and permitted destination. Include street and market waste where these are contractual responsibilities. Identify the operator responsible when a planned facility closes or equipment fails.

Cost the continuing service, including labour, vehicle maintenance, fuel, containers, transfer, disposal, monitoring and replacement. Then identify actual sources of payment: household charges, commercial charges, municipal transfers or other contracted contributions. Record billing and collection separately, because issuing an invoice does not provide working capital.

Make affordability support visible. If the public authority expects an operator to serve households that cannot pay, the contract needs a funded mechanism for that obligation. Concealing it within optimistic collection assumptions makes both service coverage and operator solvency harder to assess.

The materials account

Begin with the saleable output, not the incoming waste tonnage. Test composition, contamination, moisture, seasonal variation, sorting losses and buyer specifications. Material described as recyclable may have no accessible buyer at an acceptable delivered price.

Calculate net proceeds after collection allocations, sorting, processing, storage, rejected loads and transport. Document ownership of materials and the point at which a buyer accepts them. A gross commodity quotation is not the cash available to fund municipal operations.

Keep producer-responsibility receipts, grants and commodity receipts distinct. Each has its own eligibility and timing. The contract should state who carries an interruption in scheme payments or the loss of a major buyer, rather than treating every income line as equally dependable.

The link between the accounts

An explicit transfer from materials income can reduce the public funding requirement. It should enter the base budget only to the extent supported by a defensible downside case. Additional recovery revenue can fund expansion or reserves without being necessary to keep essential routes operating.

This arrangement does not require one ownership or procurement model. A municipal operator, contracted collector, cooperative or private facility can use the same accounting distinction. What matters is that responsibility, payment and performance remain traceable across organisational boundaries.

CONTRACTING FOR COVERAGE AND CONTROL

A tonnes-only collection contract can leave important service questions unanswered. More collected tonnes do not establish regular access for peripheral neighbourhoods, and a heavier load can reflect higher moisture or contamination. Contracts should reconcile route completion, complaints, weighed movements and destination acceptance.

At a minimum, define the evidence supporting payment, the treatment of missed collections and the process for verifying disputed performance. Maintain auditable load records across transfer and disposal interfaces. Independent spot checks can complement operator records without pretending that a digital tracking system alone proves compliant disposal.

Residual management should remain a funded obligation after valuable materials are removed. Otherwise the commercial part of the system can appear successful while rejected or low-value waste accumulates elsewhere. Facility appraisal should include realistic downtime, maintenance, permit conditions and alternative destinations.

There is also a risk in guaranteeing excessive feedstock to treatment infrastructure. A rigid minimum-volume commitment can conflict with prevention and separate recovery. Public authorities should test these incentives before accepting long-term liabilities, and distinguish a sensible availability payment from protection against every commercial risk.

WORKERS AND HOUSEHOLDS IN THE TRANSITION

UNEP's 2024 outlook warns that formalisation can remove existing waste workers' access to materials on which their livelihoods depend. It also recognises their practical knowledge and exposure to dangerous conditions. This is a reason to examine the design of transition, rather than to equate informality with either an ideal system or a problem solved by exclusion. [9]

Preparation should map collectors, sorters, aggregators and downstream buyers before reallocating rights. Ask who controls valuable materials, who performs unpaid or underpaid work, and which safety costs are excluded from commercial margins. Consultation needs to influence access, remuneration and working arrangements before procurement fixes them.

Possible arrangements include negotiated collection roles, service payments, cooperative participation and safer sorting access. Their suitability depends on local conditions and worker preferences. This paper does not establish that one form of formalisation consistently improves earnings or security.

Households also need a credible service proposition. Charges are easier to evaluate when frequency, complaints handling and support for inability to pay are clear. Enforcement without a workable collection option can displace dumping rather than resolve it; whether that occurs in the cases examined here has not been measured.

AN AGENDA FOR CAPITAL AND IMPLEMENTATION

  • Municipalities should establish the service obligation and its recurring funding before specifying new assets.
  • Financiers should require downside cases for material income and continuity arrangements for residual waste.
  • Producer schemes and operators should disclose the covered costs and the conditions for payment.

The first commissionable assignment is a service-and-cash-flow baseline for one defined urban area. Reconcile sampled route performance, weighed loads, destination records, invoices, actual receipts and operator expenditure. Include enough seasonal observation to avoid designing a permanent service around a short period of unusually favourable conditions.

The second is a materials-market study based on buyer specifications and accepted deliveries. Trace the costs and ownership of representative material flows from source to buyer. Identify the difference between an expression of purchasing interest and a contract capable of supporting facility finance.

The third is a worker and household transition assessment. Combine interviews with practical access mapping, earnings baselines, affordability analysis and complaints data. Publish the unresolved trade-offs and the party responsible for each decision, with follow-up measurement after implementation.

Public funding may be justified by cleaner neighbourhoods, environmental protection and dependable services. The case should state which benefits are expected, how they will be checked and what would lead to redesign. A recycling narrative should strengthen accountability for public spending rather than conceal its necessity.

COMMUNITIES AND THE UN SDGS

The direct classifications are SDG 11, Sustainable Cities and Communities; SDG 12, Responsible Consumption and Production; and SDG 8, Decent Work and Economic Growth. SDG 11 is primary because dependable urban collection and controlled waste management are the central question. Two Accounts for One System supports the SDG 12 mapping; Workers and Households in the Transition supports SDG 8, principally through rights, working conditions and livelihood risks.

The strongest relationships are thematic, not measured impacts. Households, waste workers and communities near transfer or disposal sites may experience different benefits and costs. Coverage, worker earnings and safety, affordability, destination compliance and environmental conditions need separate verification before claims about improvement can be made. No community or worker interviews were undertaken for this desk study.

Goals 3, 6, 10 and 13 have conditional relationships through exposure, drainage and receiving waters, access and distribution, and emissions. Goals 9, 14, 15 and 16 arise as infrastructure, environmental or accountability questions without a separate goal-specific outcome assessment. Goals 1, 2, 4, 5, 7 and 17 receive the lowest visual treatment because this paper does not establish direct relevance sufficient for a distinct assessment. These broader associations are not additional website tags.

SDG relevance and relative prominence are StoneComms interpretations of issues and outcomes documented in this research. They are not formal impact measurements, and they do not imply endorsement by the United Nations.

CONCLUSION

African waste systems need both a viable materials economy and a dependable public service. Kampala makes the collection and payment design visible; Senegal places several operating stages and worker transition within a wider programme; Petco illustrates a distinct financing mechanism for defined packaging recovery. Their differences help identify which risks a proposed investment must actually solve.

The central discipline is to identify the payer for each obligation and test the revenue at the point where it becomes usable cash. Material recovery can contribute to service funding, but its gross value cannot settle the municipal operating account. Credible circular investment begins with that distinction.
fieldData.methodology:
METHODOLOGY

Public-source comparative desk research completed on 19 November 2026. The evidence set comprises World Bank data documentation, dated KCCA announcements and its client charter, PROMOGED programme and preparation material, Petco's published fee mechanism and UNEP's waste outlook. Cases were selected for different financing functions, not representativeness or comparable performance.

The unit of analysis is the obligation-payment relationship across collection, transfer, recovery and residual management. No city-level financial model, original survey or quantitative cross-country ranking was constructed. The paired-account framework is StoneComms interpretation of the cited sources, offered as a preparation method requiring testing against actual contracts and audited operating records.
fieldData.limitations:
LIMITATIONS

Public announcements describe plans and institutional intentions without proving sustained operating results. Kampala's capacity figures are not actual collected tonnage; Senegal's preparation milestones do not establish a completed PPP; Petco's explanation concerns a defined scheme rather than all South African waste. Older institutional pages and current dated announcements are not treated as one reporting period.

Comparable audited costs, household payment data, buyer contracts, compliance records and livelihood evaluations were unavailable in this source set. No field inspection, stakeholder interview, legal assessment or investment valuation was conducted. Technology choices, statutory duties and financing suitability require local professional assessment; the report is informational research rather than legal, engineering or investment advice.
